# Chapter 5: Creating Playlists, Crates, and Smart Lists

## From a Rough Sketch to a Ready‑to‑Play Set  

Imagine you’ve been hired to DJ a wedding reception. The bride’s “first dance” song is a classic ballad, the late‑night crowd will want a high‑energy EDM banger, and the cocktail hour calls for smooth lounge tracks. You have a library of 5,000 songs, but you only have 30 minutes to assemble three distinct sections of the night. How do you pull the right tracks out of the chaos, arrange them in the order you need, and make sure they’re instantly accessible when the lights go down?  

The answer lies in **playlists, crates, and smart lists**—the three organizational tools Rekordbox gives you to turn a massive collection into a performance‑ready roadmap. This chapter walks you through creating each type, populating them efficiently, shaping them with sorting and filtering, and finally exporting your selections to a USB stick ready for Performance mode.

---

## 1. Manual Playlists and Crates  

### 1.1 What’s the Difference?  

- **Playlist** – A flat list of tracks that appears in the *Playlists* pane. Playlists are the simplest way to group songs for a particular gig or mood.  
- **Crate** – A more flexible container that can hold playlists, sub‑crates, and even other crates. Crates live in the *Explorer* view and are useful for hierarchical organization (e.g., “Wedding → Cocktail → Lounge”).  

Both behave the same way when you drag tracks onto them, but crates give you a folder‑like structure that can mirror the way you think about a set.

### 1.2 Creating a New Playlist  

1. Open the **Playlists** panel (normally on the left side of the screen).  
2. Click the **+** button at the top of the panel. A dialog appears.  
3. Type a descriptive name, e.g., *“Wedding – Cocktail Hour”*.  
4. Press **Enter**. The new playlist shows up instantly, ready for tracks.

> **Tip:** Use a consistent naming convention such as *Event‑Section‑Mood* (e.g., *Wedding‑Opening‑Chill*) so you can locate playlists quickly with the search bar.

### 1.3 Creating a New Crate  

1. Switch to the **Explorer** view (the folder icon near the top‑right).  
2. Right‑click in the blank area of the Explorer pane and choose **Create New Crate**.  
3. Name the crate (e.g., *“Wedding”*).  
4. To add sub‑crates, right‑click the newly created *Wedding* crate and select **Create New Crate** again. Name these *“Ceremony”*, *“Cocktail”*, *“Reception”*, etc.

Now you have a folder hierarchy that mirrors the event timeline.

### 1.4 Adding Tracks: Drag‑and‑Drop and Keyboard Shortcuts  

#### Drag‑and‑Drop  

- **From the Collection**: Click a track (or hold **Shift** / **Ctrl** to select multiple tracks), drag it onto the target playlist or crate, and release.  
- **From the Preview Deck**: While a track is playing in the preview deck, click the **+** button that appears on the deck’s header and choose the destination playlist/crate.

#### Keyboard Shortcuts  

- **Add to Playlist**: Select a track and press **Ctrl + Shift + P** (Windows) or **⌘ + Shift + P** (macOS). A dialog lets you pick an existing playlist or create a new one on the fly.  
- **Add to Crate**: Select a track and press **Ctrl + Shift + C** (Windows) or **⌘ + Shift + C** (macOS). Choose the target crate from the list that appears.

> **Pro tip:** When you’re in the middle of browsing a genre folder, use **Ctrl + A** to select all tracks, then apply one of the shortcuts to dump the entire batch into a crate in a single keystroke.

### 1.5 Quick‑Tagging for Visual Cues  

Rekordbox lets you assign **colors** and **rating stars** to tracks. Use these visual tags to reinforce the purpose of a playlist or crate:

- **Red** – High‑energy, peak‑time tracks.  
- **Blue** – Chill or background music.  
- **Green** – Transitional tracks that bridge different BPM ranges.

Set a color by right‑clicking a track → **Color → Choose**. Rating stars are set via the **Rating** column (click the star icons). These tags become handy when you later sort or filter within a list.

---

## 2. Shaping Playlists: Sorting and Filtering  

A playlist is only as useful as the order you can retrieve tracks from it. Rekordbox offers several built‑in ways to rearrange and narrow down the view.

### 2.1 Sorting Tracks  

Click any column header in the playlist view to sort by that attribute. Common sort options for DJs include:

| Column | Typical Use |
|--------|-------------|
| **BPM** | Group tracks by tempo for smoother beat‑matching. |
| **Key** | Keep harmonic mixes together (e.g., all tracks in C‑minor). |
| **Rating** | Push your favorite, most‑tested tracks to the top. |
| **Genre** | Separate house from techno or hip‑hop. |

You can **multi‑sort** by holding **Shift** while clicking additional columns. For example, first sort by **BPM**, then **Key** to create a BPM‑ordered, key‑grouped list.

### 2.2 Filtering Tracks  

Filtering lets you temporarily hide tracks that don’t meet a criterion, without altering the underlying playlist.

- **Search Bar**: Type a keyword (e.g., “piano”) to instantly filter tracks whose title, artist, or tags contain that word.  
- **Filter Panel**: Click the funnel icon next to the playlist name. You’ll see checkboxes for **Key**, **BPM range**, **Rating**, **Genre**, etc. Tick the boxes that apply and set the ranges.  

> **Example:** In the *“Wedding – Reception”* playlist, you might filter to only show tracks with **Rating ≥ 4** and **BPM ≥ 120** when you’re looking for high‑energy songs.

### 2.3 Saving a Filtered View  

If you often need the same filtered view, create a **smart playlist** (covered next) that captures the same criteria automatically. However, for a one‑off quick view, you can **pin** the filter:

1. After setting your filter, click the **Pin** icon in the filter panel.  
2. The filtered view stays active even if you add new tracks to the playlist later—those new tracks will appear automatically if they meet the filter.

---

## 3. Smart Playlists: Dynamic, Criteria‑Based Lists  

A **smart playlist** (sometimes called a *smart list*) is a virtual collection that updates automatically whenever tracks in your library meet the defined rules. Think of it as a “saved search” that lives alongside your manual playlists.

### 3.1 Creating a Smart Playlist  

1. In the **Playlists** pane, click the **+** button and choose **Create Smart Playlist**.  
2. The **Smart Playlist Builder** dialog opens. Here you’ll define the logic that determines which tracks belong.

### 3.2 Defining Criteria  

You can combine multiple conditions using **AND** (all must be true) or **OR** (any can be true). Each condition uses one of Rekordbox’s track metadata fields.

#### Common Criteria for DJs  

| Field | Example Condition |
|-------|-------------------|
| **BPM** | `BPM is between 124 and 130` |
| **Key** | `Key is C Minor` |
| **Rating** | `Rating is greater than or equal to 4` |
| **Genre** | `Genre contains "House"` |
| **Color** | `Color is Red` |
| **Date Added** | `Date Added is within last 30 days` |

#### Building a Sample Smart Playlist  

*Goal:* A high‑energy house set for the late‑night part of the wedding.

1. **Condition 1:** `BPM is between 124 and 130` (typical house tempo).  
2. **Condition 2:** `Key is C Minor OR Key is G Minor` (harmonic compatibility).  
3. **Condition 3:** `Rating is greater than or equal to 4`.  

Set the logical operator to **AND** between Condition 1 and Condition 3, and **OR** between the two key conditions. The builder will read it as:

> **(BPM 124‑130) AND (Rating ≥ 4) AND (Key = C Minor OR G Minor)**

Give the playlist a name, e.g., *“Wedding – Late Night House”*, and click **OK**. The list populates instantly with any tracks that satisfy the rules.

### 3.3 Editing an Existing Smart Playlist  

Right‑click the smart playlist and select **Edit Smart Playlist**. Adjust criteria, add new rules, or change the logical operators. The list updates in real time, so you can see the impact of each change instantly.

### 3.4 Using Smart Playlists in Set Planning  

Because smart playlists are always current, they’re perfect for:

- **Last‑minute track hunting:** If a guest requests a specific BPM range, you can quickly toggle the smart playlist’s BPM filter.  
- **Testing new music:** Add freshly imported tracks to the library; any that meet your existing criteria appear automatically, letting you audition them without manual sorting.  
- **Dynamic export:** When you export a smart playlist to USB, Rekordbox writes the current snapshot of matching tracks—no extra steps needed.

---

## 4. Managing Multiple Playlists and Crates  

### 4.1 Nesting Playlists Inside Crates  

You can drag a playlist into a crate to keep related lists together. For the wedding scenario:

- **Crate:** *Wedding*  
  - **Sub‑crate:** *Ceremony*  
  - **Sub‑crate:** *Cocktail* (contains playlists *“Cocktail – Chill”* and *“Cocktail – Background”*)  
  - **Sub‑crate:** *Reception* (contains playlists *“Reception – Opening”*, *“Reception – Peak”*, *“Reception – Late Night”*)

This hierarchy appears in the **Explorer** view, giving you a quick tree‑like navigation.

### 4.2 Duplicating Playlists  

If you need a similar set with slight variations (e.g., a “Cocktail – Chill” list for a different venue), right‑click the playlist and choose **Duplicate**. Rename the copy and adjust its contents. This avoids rebuilding a list from scratch.

### 4.3 Exporting Multiple Playlists at Once  

When you’re ready to take your organized lists to the hardware:

1. Insert a formatted USB drive (FAT32 or exFAT).  
2. In Rekordbox, click the **Export** mode button (top‑right).  
3. In the left pane, select the **Crate** or **Playlist** you want to export. You can hold **Ctrl** (Windows) or **⌘** (macOS) to select several items.  
4. Click the **Export** button (arrow icon) and choose the USB drive as the destination.  

Rekordbox will copy the audio files, along with cue points, beatgrid data, and playlist metadata, into the USB’s folder structure. When you plug the USB into a CDJ or DMR unit, the playlists appear as separate **Playlists** in Performance mode, ready to be loaded onto a deck.

### 4.4 Verifying the Export  

After the export finishes:

- Open the USB’s **rekordbox** folder on your computer. You’ll see a **PLAYLIST** folder containing `.m3u` files that correspond to each exported playlist.  
- Insert the USB into a CDJ/DMR, switch to **Performance** mode, and scroll the **PLAYLIST** list. Load a track from each playlist to confirm that the correct songs are present and that cue points survived the transfer.

---

## 5. Practical Workflow: Building a Wedding Set in 30 Minutes  

1. **Create Crates** – *Wedding → Ceremony, Cocktail, Reception* (5 minutes).  
2. **Add Rough Selections** – Drag all tracks tagged **Red** (high‑energy) into *Reception → Peak* playlist; drag **Blue** tracks into *Cocktail → Chill* (10 minutes).  
3. **Refine with Smart Playlists** – Build a smart playlist *“Reception – Late Night House”* using BPM and key criteria (5 minutes). Drag the smart playlist into the *Reception* crate.  
4. **Sort & Filter** – In *Reception – Peak*, sort by **Rating** descending, then filter out any tracks with **BPM < 120** (5 minutes).  
5. **Export** – Select the *Wedding* crate, hit **Export**, and write to USB (5 minutes).  

By the end of the half‑hour, you have a hierarchical crate structure that mirrors the event flow, with manually curated playlists for the unique moments and smart playlists that automatically stay up‑to‑date as you add new music later.

---

## 6. Troubleshooting Quick Tips  

| Symptom | Likely Cause | Fix |
|---------|--------------|-----|
| **Tracks missing from exported playlist** | Files not physically copied (e.g., location outside the library) | Ensure the tracks are **Analyzed** and stored on a drive accessible to Rekordbox before exporting. |
| **Smart playlist shows no results** | Criteria too restrictive (e.g., BPM range that no track matches) | Temporarily broaden the criteria or use the **Search** field to confirm that matching tracks exist. |
| **Sorting resets after closing Rekordbox** | Sorting was applied only to the current view, not saved | Click the **Save Sort** button (disk icon) in the playlist header before exiting. |
| **USB does not appear on CDJ/DMR** | USB formatted with an unsupported file system (e.g., NTFS) | Reformat the drive to **FAT32** (≤ 32 GB) or **exFAT** for larger drives. |

---

## Key Takeaways  

- **Playlists** give you flat, quick‑access lists; **crates** let you nest playlists and sub‑crates for hierarchical organization.  
- Add tracks efficiently with **drag‑and‑drop**, **Ctrl + Shift + P/C**, or the **+** button on the preview deck.  
- Use **colors** and **ratings** as visual shortcuts to identify energy levels or favorite tracks.  
- **Sorting** (by BPM, key, rating, etc.) and **filtering** (search bar, filter panel) let you reshape a playlist on the fly.  
- **Smart playlists** are dynamic collections defined by criteria such as BPM range, key, rating, or color; they update automatically as your library grows.  
- Exporting playlists or entire crates to a USB stick creates ready‑to‑play **Playlists** in Performance mode, preserving cue points and beatgrid data.  
- A disciplined workflow—crate creation, quick manual curation, smart‑list refinement, then export—turns a massive library into a set‑ready toolkit in minutes.

---

# Chapter 6: Beatgrid, Cue Points, and Loop Fundamentals

## A Real‑World Wake‑Up Call  

Imagine you’re on the decks at a weekend bar, the crowd is vibing, and you cue up a track that you know will keep the energy high. As the first beat drops, the track’s rhythm seems to slip—your foot‑tap feels out of sync, and the next song you try to blend in starts a fraction of a beat early. The culprit? An **incorrect beatgrid**.  

In this moment, the difference between a seamless mix and a jarring stumble often comes down to three simple tools you already have in Rekordbox: the **beatgrid**, **cue points**, and **loops**. Mastering how to read, edit, and employ them will give you the timing precision you need to keep the dance floor moving.  

Below we’ll explore each tool from the ground up, walk through practical editing steps, and finish with a hands‑on exercise that lets you apply what you’ve learned in a simulated mix.

---

## 1. The Beatgrid – Your Timing Blueprint  

### 1.1 What the Beatgrid Is  
When Rekordbox analyzes a track (see *Importing and Analyzing Your Music Library*), it creates a visual representation of the track’s rhythmic structure known as the **beatgrid**. Think of it as a ruler laid over the waveform, with vertical lines marking every beat. The first line—called the **downbeat**—marks the start of a musical bar and is the anchor point for all subsequent beats.

| Symbol | Meaning |
|--------|---------|
| **▉▉▉▉** | Downbeat (the first beat of each bar) |
| **|** | Regular beat markers (quarter‑note intervals) |
| **–** | Sub‑beat divisions (eighth‑ or sixteenth‑note) |

When the grid aligns perfectly with the music, Rekordbox can accurately calculate the **BPM** (beats per minute) and keep your decks in sync, whether you use **Sync** or manual beat‑matching.

### 1.2 Why a Correct Beatgrid Matters  

- **Consistent Beatmatching** – A misaligned grid forces you to adjust timing manually, increasing the risk of phase errors.  
- **Reliable Looping** – Loops snap to grid lines; an offset grid creates loops that drift or cut off the groove.  
- **Accurate Cue Placement** – Cue points placed on a wrong grid will trigger a fraction of a beat early or late.  

### 1.3 Spotting Common Beatgrid Errors  

1. **Drift** – The grid gradually moves away from the waveform, often visible after the first 30–60 seconds.  
2. **Offset** – The entire grid is shifted forward or backward, usually by a fraction of a beat.  
3. **Double/Half Tempo** – Rekordbox may have interpreted the track’s BPM as twice or half its real value, causing the grid to double‑speed or halve‑speed the beats.  

### 1.4 Editing the Beatgrid in Rekordbox  

> **Tip:** All beatgrid edits are made in the **Edit** mode of the track’s waveform view. If you’re unsure where to find it, refer back to *Navigating the Rekordbox Interface*.

#### Step‑by‑Step Guide  

1. **Open the Track**  
   - Double‑click the track in the **Collection** or a **Playlist** to bring up the waveform.  

2. **Enter Grid‑Edit Mode**  
   - Click the **Grid** icon (looks like a ruler) or press **Ctrl + G** (Windows) / **⌘ + G** (Mac).  

3. **Set the Downbeat**  
   - Locate the first strong kick or snare that marks the start of the first bar.  
   - Drag the **first grid line** (the downbeat) so it snaps exactly onto that transient.  

4. **Adjust the BPM if Needed**  
   - If the grid is moving too fast or too slow, click the **BPM** value and type the correct number, or use the **+ / –** buttons to nudge it.  

5. **Fine‑Tune the Grid Position**  
   - Use the **Shift‑Left/Shift‑Right** arrows to move the entire grid forward or backward in 1‑beat increments.  
   - For sub‑beat precision, hold **Alt** (Windows) / **Option** (Mac) while dragging.  

6. **Correct Drift**  
   - Play the track and watch the grid lines. If they start to separate from the waveform after a minute, pause, and click the **“Set Grid”** button at the point where the drift begins. This tells Rekordbox to re‑anchor the grid from that position onward.  

7. **Confirm and Save**  
   - Click **OK** or press **Enter** to apply changes. The updated grid is now stored in the track’s metadata and will be used every time the track loads.  

#### Quick‑Check Checklist  

- [ ] Downbeat aligns with the first kick/snare.  
- [ ] Grid lines stay locked to the waveform throughout the track.  
- [ ] BPM matches the track’s perceived tempo (tap the tempo if unsure).  

### 1.5 Saving Your Work  

Rekordbox automatically writes grid changes to the track’s **.rekordbox** file. However, if you plan to export the track to a USB for CDJ playback, be sure to **sync your library** (see *Exporting to USB for CDJ/DMR Playback*) so the corrected grid travels with the file.

---

## 2. Cue Points – Instant Access to Musical Landmarks  

### 2.1 What a Cue Point Is  

A **cue point** marks a specific moment in a track that you can jump to instantly with the **Cue** button on your controller or the on‑screen button. Unlike **Hot Cues**, which are stored as separate playback positions, a basic cue point is a single, global marker that resets the track to the exact same spot each time you press Cue.

### 2.2 Setting Your First Cue  

1. **Load the Track** onto Deck 1 (or Deck 2).  
2. **Play** the track and listen for the moment you want to cue – commonly the start of a phrase, a vocal hook, or the first downbeat after an intro.  
3. **Pause** at that exact spot.  
4. Click the **Cue** button on the screen (or the corresponding hardware button). The button will light up, indicating the cue point is stored.  

> **Pro tip:** If you accidentally set the cue a few milliseconds early, you can nudge it forward using the **Cue‑Nudge** controls (usually **← / →** on the controller) while the cue is active.

### 2.3 Managing Multiple Cue Points  

Rekordbox allows you to store **up to 8 cue points per track** (the same number as Hot Cues, but they behave differently). To add more:

- **Shift + Cue** (or the **+** button) creates a new cue at the current playback position.  
- To **rename** a cue, right‑click the cue marker on the waveform, select **Rename**, and type a descriptive label (e.g., “Breakdown Start”).  
- **Delete** a cue by right‑clicking and choosing **Delete**, or select the cue and press **Del** on the keyboard.  

### 2.4 Using Cue Points in a Live Mix  

| Situation | Cue Point Strategy |
|-----------|--------------------|
| **Intro to a new track** | Set a cue at the first downbeat of the intro; press Cue as the previous track ends. |
| **Jumping to a breakdown** | Place a cue at the exact moment the breakdown begins; trigger it to surprise the crowd. |
| **Re‑entering after a loop** | Use a cue right after the loop’s exit point to resume the track cleanly. |

Because cue points are anchored to the beatgrid, they stay perfectly in time even if you change the track’s tempo with the **Pitch Fader**. This makes them indispensable for quick, reliable transitions.

---

## 3. Loops – Shaping the Groove in Real Time  

### 3.1 Loop Basics  

A **loop** repeats a selected segment of a track over and over until you release it. In Rekordbox, loops snap to the beatgrid, ensuring the repeated segment always starts and ends on a beat. The most common loop lengths are:

- **1/4** (one beat) – great for stutter effects or quick chops.  
- **1/2** (two beats) – useful for building short rhythmic variations.  
- **1 bar** (4 beats) – the standard length for extending a phrase.  

You can also create **custom loops** of any length by setting the start and end points manually.

### 3.2 Creating a Loop  

#### Using the Auto‑Loop Buttons  

1. **Play** the track and locate the point where you want the loop to begin.  
2. Press the **Auto‑Loop** button that matches the desired length (e.g., **1/4**, **1/2**, **1 Bar**). The loop will instantly appear and start repeating.  

#### Manual Loop In/Out  

1. **Press the “Loop In”** button (usually labeled **IN**) at the exact start point.  
2. **Press the “Loop Out”** button (**OUT**) where you want the loop to end.  
3. The loop automatically activates.  

> **Note:** Manual loops give you full control over length and placement, ideal for custom phrasing.

### 3.3 Activating, Extending, and Exiting Loops  

- **Activate** a pre‑set loop by pressing the **Loop** button again; the track will jump to the loop’s start point and begin repeating.  
- **Extend** a loop on the fly by holding the **Loop‑In** or **Loop‑Out** button while the loop is active; the grid will expand the loop forward or backward in beat increments.  
- **Exit** a loop by pressing the **Loop** button a second time, or by using the **Loop‑Roll** function (see below) to keep the loop playing while the rest of the track continues in the background.  

### 3.4 Loop‑Roll – Keeping the Energy Flowing  

The **Loop‑Roll** feature lets you “roll” a loop for a set number of beats while the track continues its normal progression underneath. This is perfect for creating tension before a drop or for layering a vocal phrase over a repeating instrumental.

**How to use Loop‑Roll:**  

1. Set a loop of any length.  
2. Press the **Loop‑Roll** button (often a small circular icon).  
3. The loop will repeat for a predefined number of beats (default is 4 bars) and then automatically release, allowing the track to resume.  

You can adjust the roll length in Rekordbox’s preferences if you need longer or shorter rolls.

### 3.5 Practical Looping Tips for Beginners  

- **Start Small:** Practice with 1/4 and 1/2 loops to get comfortable with timing.  
- **Listen for Phrase Endings:** Align loop points with musical phrases (e.g., at the start of a vocal line) to avoid abrupt cuts.  
- **Combine with Cue Points:** Set a cue just after a loop’s exit point; this gives you a clean “hand‑off” back to the main track.  

---

## 4. Putting It All Together – A Simulated Mix Exercise  

Now that you’ve seen each tool in isolation, let’s apply them in a short, structured practice session. This exercise assumes you have a **controller** or **keyboard** connected and that you’re working in **Performance Mode** (see the earlier chapter on *Performance‑Ready Engine*).

### 4.1 Preparation  

1. **Select Two Tracks** – Choose a track with a clear, steady beat (Track A) and a second track with a contrasting energy level (Track B).  
2. **Analyze Both Tracks** – If you haven’t already, run **Analyze** on both to generate BPM and beatgrid data.  

### 4.2 Step‑by‑Step Mix  

| Step | Action | Goal |
|------|--------|------|
| **1** | Open Track A, verify its beatgrid using the method in **Section 1.5**. Correct any drift. | Ensure timing foundation is solid. |
| **2** | Set a **cue point** at the first downbeat of Track A’s intro. Name it “Start”. | Quick start and reference point. |
| **3** | Create a **1‑bar loop** on the last four beats of Track A’s intro (just before the first major drop). | Extend the intro while you prepare the next track. |
| **4** | Activate **Loop‑Roll** for 2 bars, then release. | Build tension before the transition. |
| **5** | Load Track B on the second deck, set a **cue point** at its first downbeat (label “Drop”). | Ready the incoming track. |
| **6** | While Track A’s loop‑roll is still playing, **beat‑match** Track B using the pitch fader and visual grid. | Practice manual beatmatching with visual aid. |
| **7** | Press **Cue** on Deck 2 at the “Drop” cue point, then **cross‑fade** to Deck 2 as the loop‑roll ends. | Execute a clean transition using cue points. |
| **8** | After the transition, set a **1/2‑beat loop** on the first two beats of Track B’s chorus. | Reinforce the new groove and experiment with loop length. |
| **9** | Exit the loop after 4 bars, letting the track run out. | Return to full track flow. |
| **10** | Review the waveform of both tracks, confirming that all cue points and loops are correctly aligned with the beatgrid. | Consolidate learning and spot any missed errors. |

### 4.3 Reflection Questions  

- Did any of the loops feel “off‑beat”? If so, check the underlying beatgrid for hidden drift.  
- How smoothly did the cue‑point transition feel? Could a different cue placement improve the flow?  
- Were you able to keep the tempo stable while adjusting the pitch fader during beatmatching?  

Answering these questions will help you internalize the relationship between beatgrid accuracy, cue placement, and loop timing.

---

## Key Takeaways  

- The **beatgrid** is the rhythmic backbone of every track; a correctly aligned grid guarantees reliable **BPM**, **cue**, and **loop** behavior.  
- **Editing the beatgrid** involves setting the downbeat, adjusting tempo, and correcting drift—use the Grid‑Edit mode and the step‑by‑step workflow outlined above.  
- **Cue points** provide instant, repeatable access to crucial musical moments; they are anchored to the beatgrid, making them robust under tempo changes.  
- **Loops** (1/4, 1/2, 1‑bar, custom) let you repeat sections of a track in time with the grid; **Loop‑Roll** adds a temporary, rhythmic “roll” that enhances phrasing.  
- Practicing a structured mix—checking grids, setting cues, and employing loops—builds the muscle memory needed for confident live performance.  

By mastering these three fundamentals, you gain the precision required to keep the dance floor moving, no matter how complex the next track may be. Happy mixing!

# Chapter 7: Advanced Track Preparation: Hot Cues and Slicers

## Why Hot Cues and Slicers Are Game‑Changers  

Imagine you’re halfway through a set and the crowd’s energy spikes. You want to jump to a killer vocal hook **exactly** where the beat drops, but you’re still on the previous phrase. With a well‑prepared hot cue you can drop straight onto that moment with a single button press—no hunting, no hesitation.  

The **slicer** takes that power a step further. By pre‑cutting a track into rhythmic “slices,” you can trigger any part of the song like a drum pad, creating on‑the‑fly edits or building a new groove without leaving your deck.  

Both tools turn a static track into a **performance instrument**, letting you react instantly to the dancefloor while keeping your mix tight and musical.

---

## Assigning Hot Cues and Giving Them Meaningful Labels  

### 1. Locate the Cue Panel  

1. Load a track onto Deck 1 (or Deck 2).  
2. In the **Track View** (the central waveform area), you’ll see the **Cue** section just below the waveform.  
3. Click the **Hot Cue** button (the square icon with a “+”) to open the first empty slot.

> *Tip:* If you don’t see the Cue panel, press **Ctrl + 1** (Windows) or **⌘ + 1** (Mac) to toggle it on.

### 2. Set the Cue Point  

1. Play the track and pause at the exact moment you want to jump to—commonly the start of a phrase, a vocal line, a drum hit, or a melodic hook.  
2. Press **Hot Cue 1** (or the numbered button on your controller) to store that position.  

> **Hot Cue** = a user‑defined point in the track that can be recalled instantly.

### 3. Label the Cue  

1. Right‑click the newly created hot cue marker on the waveform.  
2. Choose **Rename** and type a short, descriptive label, e.g., **“Vox Intro”**, **“Kick Drop”**, or **“Break‑2”**.  
3. Press **Enter** to confirm.  

> **Best practice:** Keep labels under 12 characters so they’re readable on small controller screens.

### 4. Choose a Color (Optional)  

1. Right‑click the cue again and select **Color** → pick a hue that matches your mental map (e.g., red for energy peaks, blue for mellow sections).  
2. The colored bar will appear on the waveform, giving you a visual cue at a glance.

### 5. Add More Hot Cues  

Repeat steps 2‑4 for each critical moment. A typical beginner’s layout might look like:

| Hot Cue | Label      | Color |
|---------|------------|-------|
| 1       | Intro Vox  | Yellow|
| 2       | Drop Kick  | Red   |
| 3       | Bridge FX  | Purple|
| 4       | Outro Loop | Green |

---

## Using the Slicer Function to Trigger Sample Slices  

### What Is a Slicer?  

The **slicer** automatically divides a track into evenly spaced beats (or bars) and assigns each slice to a pad on your controller. Think of it as a built‑in sampler that respects the track’s **beatgrid**—the timing map you already set up in Chapter 6.

### 1. Activate the Slicer  

1. With the track loaded, click the **Slicer** icon (a grid of nine squares) located in the lower‑right of the Track View.  
2. The waveform will now display vertical slice markers (typically 16 or 32 per track, depending on the BPM and length).  

### 2. Choose a Slice Mode  

Rekordbox offers three preset slice lengths:

| Mode | Description |
|------|-------------|
| **1‑Bar** | One musical bar per slice (good for melodic loops). |
| **2‑Beat** | Two beats per slice (ideal for drum‑oriented chops). |
| **4‑Beat** | Four beats per slice (captures whole phrases). |

Select the mode that matches the style you intend to remix.

### 3. Map Slices to Your Controller  

1. Open **Preferences** → **Controller** → **MIDI Mapping**.  
2. Click **Learn**, then press a pad on your controller.  
3. In the mapping window, choose **Slicer – Slice 1**, **Slice 2**, etc., until all desired pads are assigned.  

> **Note:** Most modern DJ controllers come pre‑mapped for the slicer, but double‑checking guarantees the pads fire the correct slices.

### 4. Triggering Slices Live  

During a performance, simply hit the pad assigned to **Slice 5** (for example) and the corresponding audio segment will jump out, overlaying the currently playing track. You can layer multiple slices, creating rhythmic stabs or melodic bursts on the fly.

### 5. Fine‑Tuning Slice Points  

If the automatic slice markers don’t line up perfectly with the music:

1. Click **Edit Slices** (pencil icon) in the slicer view.  
2. Drag individual slice markers left or right until they sit on the exact beat you want.  
3. Press **Enter** to lock the changes.

---

## Storing Memory Cues for Later Recall  

### What Is a Memory Cue?  

A **memory cue** is a cue point that lives **outside** the track file itself. It’s stored in Rekordbox’s database, allowing you to experiment without altering the original track’s hot cues. This is especially handy when you’re still testing where the best cue spots should be.

### 1. Create a Memory Cue  

1. While the track is playing, press **Ctrl + M** (Windows) or **⌘ + M** (Mac).  
2. The cue point appears as a **blue** marker (different from the hot cue colors).  

### 2. Label and Color the Memory Cue  

Right‑click the blue marker → **Rename** → type a label such as **“Temp Drop”**. You can also assign a color, though memory cues default to blue for easy distinction.

### 3. Convert to a Hot Cue (When Ready)  

If you decide the memory cue belongs in your performance set:

1. Right‑click the memory cue and select **Convert to Hot Cue**.  
2. Choose the hot cue slot you want it to occupy.  

### 4. Deleting or Archiving Memory Cues  

- **Delete:** Right‑click → **Delete**.  
- **Archive:** Move the track to a **“Cue‑Testing”** crate; the memory cues stay attached to the track file in the database, ready for future sessions.

---

## Organizing Hot Cues Within the Track View  

A cluttered cue layout can slow you down. Rekordbox gives you several tools to keep everything tidy.

### 1. Cue List Panel  

Open the **Cue List** (the vertical pane on the left of Track View). It displays all hot cues, memory cues, and loops for the current track in a compact list:

- **Number** – hot cue slot.  
- **Label** – your custom name.  
- **Color** – visual cue.  

You can drag entries up or down to reorder their priority, which also changes the order they appear on your controller pads (if you use pad‑mode hot cues).

### 2. Grouping Cues by Function  

Create **Cue Groups** in the Cue List:

1. Click the **+** button at the bottom of the Cue List.  
2. Name the group, e.g., **“Energy Peaks”**.  
3. Drag relevant hot cues into that group.  

Now, when you switch to **Cue Group** mode on your controller, only those cues will be active, reducing the chance of hitting the wrong pad.

### 3. Using the “Cue Jump” Feature  

If you prefer a single button to cycle through cues:

1. Enable **Cue Jump** in **Preferences → Deck**.  
2. Assign **Cue Jump** to a pad on your controller.  
3. Pressing the pad will step through hot cues in the order they appear in the Cue List—perfect for quick improvisation.

---

## Exporting Prepared Tracks So Cue Data Travels With Them  

When you move your prepared tracks to a USB drive for CDJ/DMR playback, you need to **export** the cue data; otherwise, the hot cues and slicer settings will be lost.

### 1. Create an Export Playlist  

1. In the **Playlist** panel, right‑click and select **Create New Playlist** → name it **“Performance Set”**.  
2. Drag all tracks you’ve prepared (with hot cues, slicers, memory cues) into this playlist.

### 2. Verify Cue Data  

1. Select the playlist, then click the **Export** button (the upward arrow) in the top‑right toolbar.  
2. In the export dialog, ensure **“Include Cue Points & Loops”** and **“Include Slicer Data”** are checked.  

> These options are usually on by default, but double‑checking prevents a silent loss of data.

### 3. Choose Destination  

1. Plug in your USB stick (formatted to FAT32 or exFAT).  
2. In the export window, select the USB drive as the destination.  
3. Click **Export**.  

Rekordbox will copy the audio files **and** embed a small **.xml** file that stores all cue information. When you load the track on a CDJ, the hot cues, slicer pads, and memory cues will appear exactly as you left them.

### 4. Test the Export  

1. Eject the USB safely and insert it into a CDJ (or another computer with Rekordbox).  
2. Load a track and confirm that your hot cue labels, colors, and slicer pads are present.  

If anything is missing, return to the playlist, double‑check the export options, and repeat.

---

## A Practical Workflow: From Raw Track to Performance‑Ready Weapon  

> **Scenario:** You’re preparing for a 90‑minute house set at a local club. You have three tracks you plan to weave together: “Sunrise Groove,” “Midnight Pulse,” and “Echo Bass.”  

1. **Analyze & Beatgrid Check** – Already covered in Chapter 6; ensure each track’s BPM is locked and the beatgrid aligns with the downbeats.  
2. **Set Hot Cues**  
   - **Sunrise Groove** – Cue 1 = “Intro Vox” (0:12), Cue 2 = “Drop Kick” (1:04).  
   - **Midnight Pulse** – Cue 1 = “Build‑Up” (0:45), Cue 2 = “Break‑FX” (2:30).  
   - **Echo Bass** – Cue 1 = “Bass Hit” (0:20), Cue 2 = “Outro Loop” (3:10).  
3. **Label & Color** – Use bright yellow for vocal intros, red for high‑energy drops, purple for FX moments.  
4. **Create Slices** – Activate the slicer on each track, choose **2‑Beat** mode, and map slices to pads 1‑8 on Deck 1 and Deck 2.  
5. **Test Memory Cues** – While jamming, press **Ctrl + M** at a tentative “Bridge Kick” point in “Midnight Pulse.” After a few trials, convert it to Hot Cue 3.  
6. **Organize** – Group cues into **“Energy Peaks”** (all drops) and **“Transitions”** (intro/outro points).  
7. **Export** – Build a playlist called **“Club Set”**, export to USB with cue data enabled.  
8. **Dry‑Run** – Load the USB on a CDJ, verify all cues appear, and run a quick mock‑mix to ensure the slicer triggers correctly.  

When the night arrives, you’ll be able to:

- Jump straight to “Drop Kick” on “Sunrise Groove” with a single button.  
- Layer a 2‑beat slice from “Echo Bass” over the break in “Midnight Pulse,” creating a fresh groove on the spot.  
- Use the **Cue Jump** pad to cycle through transition cues without looking at the screen, keeping your eyes on the crowd.

---

## Troubleshooting Common Issues  

| Symptom | Likely Cause | Quick Fix |
|---------|--------------|-----------|
| Hot cue doesn’t fire on the controller | Pad not mapped or mapping lost after software restart | Re‑enter **MIDI Mapping** mode, assign the pad again, and **Save** the mapping. |
| Slicer slices are out of sync with the beat | Beatgrid misaligned or wrong slice mode selected | Re‑check the beatgrid in the **Beatgrid** editor (Chapter 6) and select the appropriate slice mode. |
| Exported USB shows no hot cues | “Include Cue Points & Loops” unchecked during export | Re‑export, confirming the checkbox is ticked. |
| Memory cue disappears after closing Rekordbox | Track not saved to a crate; memory cues are only stored for tracks in the library | Add the track to a **crate** before creating memory cues. |
| Too many hot cues cluttering the view | Unused cues still occupying slots | Right‑click unwanted hot cues → **Delete**; keep only the cues you need for performance. |

---

## Best Practices for Long‑Term Cue Management  

- **Standardize Naming:** Adopt a simple convention, e.g., **“Vox‑Intro,” “Kick‑Drop,” “FX‑Break.”** Consistency speeds up visual scanning on both screen and controller.  
- **Color‑Code by Function:** Reserve a palette (e.g., red = energy, blue = melodic, green = loop).  
- **Back‑Up Your Library:** Periodically export the **Rekordbox Library** (Preferences → Advanced → Export Library) to a cloud folder. This preserves all cue data, slicer settings, and playlists.  
- **Limit Hot Cues per Track:** Aim for 4‑6 meaningful cues; more can lead to accidental pad presses during a live set.  
- **Test on the Target Hardware:** Cue layouts can shift between a laptop controller and a CDJ; always do a quick test run on the actual gear you’ll use.

---

## ## Key Takeaways  

- **Hot cues** let you jump instantly to crucial points; label them clearly and use colors for instant visual cues.  
- The **slicer** automatically partitions a track into beat‑aligned slices; map these to pads for on‑the‑fly sampling.  
- **Memory cues** are temporary, non‑destructive markers stored in Rekordbox’s database—great for experimentation before committing to hot cues.  
- Organize cues with the **Cue List**, **Cue Groups**, and **Cue Jump** features to keep your workflow clean and avoid mis‑fires.  
- When exporting to USB for CDJ/DMR playback, always enable **“Include Cue Points & Loops”** and **“Include Slicer Data”** to preserve your preparation.  

By mastering hot cues, slicers, and memory cues, you transform each track from a static audio file into a versatile instrument ready for any crowd‑driven moment. Happy prepping!

# Chapter 8: Performance Mode: Decks, Mixer, and Effects

## Jump‑Starting the Performance Mode

Imagine you’re setting up for a friend’s house‑party. The lights are low, the crowd is a mix of old‑school funk and fresh house, and you’ve got a laptop running Rekordbox ready to go. The moment the first track drops, you want the music to flow without a hitch—no sudden silences, no awkward volume spikes, and the ability to add a splash of delay or filter that makes the crowd react. This is exactly what the **Performance mode** in Rekordbox is built for: a live‑ready layout that puts two virtual decks, a mixer, and a suite of effects at your fingertips.

In this chapter you’ll learn how to:

1. Load tracks onto the two virtual decks and control playback.
2. Shape the sound with EQ, filter, and gain on the mixer.
3. Apply and tweak built‑in effects such as delay, reverb, and filter.
4. Map those effects to your controller’s knobs or pads for hands‑on control.
5. Use the crossfader to blend the decks smoothly.

By the end of the walkthrough you’ll be comfortable launching tracks, sculpting tone, and adding effects—all without leaving the Performance screen.

---

## 1. The Performance Mode Layout – What You See

When you click the **Performance** button on the top‑right of the Rekordbox window, the interface re‑arranges into three core zones:

| Zone | Visual Element | Primary Function |
|------|----------------|------------------|
| **Deck A** | Large waveform, transport controls (Play, Cue, Loop, Hot Cue) | Plays the first track |
| **Deck B** | Mirror of Deck A, side‑by‑side for comparison | Plays the second track |
| **Mixer** | Channel strips (EQ, Gain, Filter), crossfader, effect slots | Controls volume, tone, and effects for each deck |

Below the decks you’ll also find the **Effect Rack** (four slots per deck) and a **Sampler** area (covered later in the book). For now, focus on the three zones above—they are the heart of live mixing.

> **Tip:** If you’re using a controller (e.g., Pioneer DDJ‑400), the Performance layout will automatically map many of its physical knobs and faders to the on‑screen controls. This is called **Automatic Mapping** and saves you time during setup.

---

## 2. Loading Tracks onto the Virtual Decks

### 2.1. Selecting a Track

1. **Browse** your library in the left‑hand pane (the **Explorer** you explored in Chapter 4).  
2. **Hover** over a track thumbnail; a small **▶︎** icon appears. Click it to **preview** the track in the headphone cue (use the cue button on Deck A or B to listen).  
3. When you’re ready, **drag** the track onto the deck you want to use, or right‑click the track and choose **“Load to Deck A”** or **“Load to Deck B.”**

> **Pro tip:** Keep your most frequently used tracks in a “Ready‑to‑Play” playlist (see Chapter 5). This reduces hunting time during a set.

### 2.2. Understanding the Transport Controls

| Control | Symbol | What It Does |
|---------|--------|--------------|
| **Play** | ▶︎ | Starts playback from the current position |
| **Cue** | ● | Instantly jumps playback to the cue point (the track’s start or a manually set point) |
| **Loop In / Loop Out** | ☐ / ☐ | Sets the start and end points of a loop; the loop will repeat until you press **Loop Exit** |
| **Hot Cues** | numbered circles (1‑8) | Instantly jumps to a pre‑saved cue point; useful for quick drops or sample triggers |
| **Pitch / Tempo Slider** | horizontal bar | Adjusts playback speed (BPM) while preserving pitch (if **Key Lock** is on) |
| **Key Lock** | lock icon | Keeps the track’s musical key constant when changing tempo |

All these controls are mirrored on Deck A and Deck B, letting you prep the next track while the current one is playing.

### 2.3. Quick‑Start Workflow

1. **Load** Track 1 to Deck A and set a cue point at the first beat.  
2. **Load** Track 2 to Deck B, but keep it paused.  
3. **Set** a loop on Deck A (e.g., 4‑beat loop) to give yourself a breathing space for mixing.  
4. **Play** Deck A, then **cue** Deck B at its first beat while the loop runs. You now have both tracks ready for a smooth transition.

---

## 3. Shaping the Sound – Mixer Controls

The mixer is where you balance levels, sculpt frequencies, and apply filters. Even if you’re new to EQ, think of it as a **tone‑shaping tool** that lets you emphasize or cut certain parts of the audio spectrum.

### 3.1. Gain (Volume) Faders

- **Location:** The vertical sliders on each channel strip (Deck A and Deck B).  
- **Purpose:** Controls the overall output level for each deck.  
- **Tip:** Start each track with the gain set to **0 dB** (the default). Adjust up or down only if a track is noticeably louder or quieter than the other.

### 3.2. EQ (Equalizer) Sections

Each channel has three EQ knobs:

| EQ Band | Frequency Range | Typical Use |
|---------|----------------|-------------|
| **Low** | 20 Hz – 200 Hz | Boost for bass‑heavy tracks or cut to reduce muddiness |
| **Mid** | 200 Hz – 2 kHz | Shape the body of vocals or synths |
| **High** | 2 kHz – 20 kHz | Add sparkle to hi‑hats, cymbals, or vocal sibilance |

**How to use them in a live mix:**

1. **Cut the low** on the incoming deck (Deck B) while the outgoing deck (Deck A) is still playing. This prevents overlapping bass frequencies that can make the mix sound “boomy.”  
2. **Boost the mids** on Deck B if you want the next track’s vocals to cut through.  
3. **Add a slight high‑end boost** on Deck B as it comes in to give it presence.

Remember: **Less is more**. Small adjustments (± 2–3 dB) often sound cleaner than dramatic swings.

### 3.3. Filter Controls

- **Location:** A dedicated knob (often labeled **“Filter”** or shown as a small “⊂” icon) on each channel.  
- **Function:** Applies a **high‑pass** (cuts low frequencies) or **low‑pass** (cuts high frequencies) filter, depending on the knob’s position.  
- **Practical Use:**  
  - **High‑pass filter** on Deck B during a transition to gradually remove the bass until the next track’s bass takes over.  
  - **Low‑pass filter** on Deck A for an “out‑fade” effect—think of a classic “sweeping” transition where the music fades into a soft hiss before the next track drops.

### 3.4. Crossfader – Blending Decks Seamlessly

The **crossfader** sits horizontally below the decks, spanning from **“A”** (left) to **“B”** (right). Moving it left sends the audio solely to Deck A; moving it right sends it solely to Deck B. In the middle, both decks blend.

**Crossfader Curves**

Rekordbox lets you choose a **curve** that determines how quickly the audio fades from one deck to the other:

- **Linear:** Equal fade for both decks. Good for smooth, gradual mixes.  
- **Sharp:** Quick cut from one deck to the other. Ideal for scratching or abrupt transitions.  
- **Custom:** Adjust the curve in the Preferences > Mixer > Crossfader section.

**Basic Crossfader Technique**

1. While Deck A is playing, **cue** Deck B and set a loop if needed.  
2. As Deck A’s phrase ends (usually after 4 or 8 bars), **gradually slide** the crossfader toward Deck B.  
3. Simultaneously, **adjust the EQ** (cut low on Deck B, boost low on Deck A) to smooth the frequency overlap.  
4. Once Deck B is fully audible, **release** the crossfader back to the center and fine‑tune its EQ for the new track.

---

## 4. Adding Flavor with Built‑In Effects

Rekordbox ships with a palette of **audio effects** that can transform a plain track into a dynamic moment. Effects are grouped into **categories** (Delay, Reverb, Filter, etc.) and each deck has four **effect slots**.

### 4.1. Overview of Core Effects

| Effect | Typical Use | Parameter Highlights |
|--------|-------------|----------------------|
| **Delay** | Echoes that repeat the incoming signal | Time, Feedback, Mix |
| **Reverb** | Simulated space (room, hall) that adds depth | Size, Decay, Mix |
| **Filter** | Sweeping low‑ or high‑frequency cuts | Frequency, Resonance, Mix |
| **Phaser / Flanger** | Modulated, swirling textures | Rate, Depth, Mix |
| **Noise** | Adds static, vinyl‑style hiss | Level, Mix |
| **Gate** | Cuts the signal when it falls below a threshold | Threshold, Release, Mix |

Each effect has a **“Dry/Wet”** (or **Mix**) knob that balances the original (dry) signal with the processed (wet) signal. For live mixing, start with a **low Mix** (10–20 %) to keep the effect subtle.

### 4.2. Loading an Effect

1. **Locate** the **Effect Rack** on the right side of each deck.  
2. Click the **“+”** button in an empty slot.  
3. A dropdown appears—choose the desired effect category (e.g., **Delay**) and then the specific preset (e.g., **“Simple Echo”**).  
4. The effect’s parameters appear below the slot. Adjust them in real time while the track plays.

### 4.3. Using an Effect in a Live Transition

**Scenario:** You want to emphasize the drop of a house track with a short echo that fades into the next song.

1. **Load** a **Delay** effect on Deck B’s slot 1.  
2. Set **Time** to 1/4 note (or sync it to the track’s beat if **Sync** is enabled).  
3. Reduce **Feedback** to a low value (to avoid endless repeats).  
4. Increase **Mix** to about **30 %** just before the drop.  
5. As the beat hits, **push** the crossfader to Deck B while the echo trails off, creating a “splash” that blends the two songs.

### 4.4. Combining Effects

You can stack effects (e.g., **Filter** + **Reverb**) for richer textures. Keep the total **Mix** low for each effect; otherwise the sound may become muddy. A common live‑mix combo:

- **Filter:** High‑pass sweep on Deck A during the outro.  
- **Reverb:** Light hall reverb on Deck B as it enters, giving it space.  

Practice toggling the **On/Off** button for each effect to see how it alters the sound instantly.

---

## 5. Mapping Effects to Controller Knobs or Pads

If you’re using a DJ controller (e.g., Pioneer DDJ‑400, DDJ‑1000), you can assign effect parameters to physical knobs, faders, or pads. This gives you tactile control and frees you from mouse clicks.

### 5.1. Accessing the Mapping Interface

1. Click **Preferences** (gear icon) → **Controller** → **MIDI Mapping**.  
2. The screen splits into two panels: **“Software”** (left) and **“Hardware”** (right).  
3. **Select** the effect you want to map (e.g., **Delay → Mix**).

### 5.2. Mapping a Parameter

1. In the **Software** panel, click the **parameter** you wish to assign (e.g., the **Mix** knob of Delay).  
2. In the **Hardware** panel, click the controller element you want to use (e.g., **Knob 1** on Deck B).  
3. A confirmation appears: **“Mix → Knob 1”**.  
4. **Test** the mapping by turning the knob while the track plays; you should see the Mix level change in real time.

> **Tip:** Map the **Effect On/Off** to a pad for instant toggling, and the **Mix** to a knob for smooth fades.

### 5.3. Saving and Loading Mapping Presets

- After mapping, click **“Save”** and give the preset a name (e.g., **“Party_Echo”**).  
- You can **load** different presets for different genres or moods, allowing you to switch setups without re‑mapping each time.

### 5.4. Practical Mapping Example

| Effect | Parameter | Controller Assignment |
|--------|-----------|------------------------|
| **Delay** | Mix | Knob 2 (Deck B) |
| **Delay** | On/Off | Pad 4 (Deck B) |
| **Filter** | Frequency | Knob 1 (Deck A) |
| **Filter** | On/Off | Pad 3 (Deck A) |

Now, during a set you can **activate** the delay with a tap on Pad 4, **sweep** the mix using Knob 2, and simultaneously **filter** the outgoing track with Knob 1—all without looking at the screen.

---

## 6. Putting It All Together – A Mini‑Set Walkthrough

Below is a step‑by‑step example that combines everything covered so far. Feel free to follow along with your own music collection.

### 6.1. Preparation

1. **Select** two tracks that share a similar BPM (e.g., 124 BPM).  
2. **Load** Track 1 to Deck A, **Track 2** to Deck B.  
3. **Set** a cue point at the first beat of each track.  
4. **Create** a 4‑beat loop on Deck A (use Loop In/Out).  
5. **Assign** a **Filter** effect to Deck A’s Slot 1 and a **Delay** to Deck B’s Slot 1.  
6. **Map** the Delay Mix to Knob 2 (Deck B) and Filter Frequency to Knob 1 (Deck A) via the MIDI Mapping screen.

### 6.2. Live Mixing Sequence

| Step | Action | Reason |
|------|--------|--------|
| 1 | **Play** Deck A, let the loop run. | Gives you breathing room while preparing Deck B. |
| 2 | **Cue** Deck B at its first beat, keep it paused. | Ready to launch instantly. |
| 3 | **Turn on** the Filter effect on Deck A (pad). | Starts a high‑pass sweep to thin out the bass. |
| 4 | **Slide** the Filter Frequency knob (Knob 1) upward as the loop nears its end. | Gradually removes low frequencies, preventing clash. |
| 5 | **Press** Play on Deck B while the filter is still active. | Deck B now enters with a clean low‑end. |
| 6 | **Move** the crossfader from A to B over 2‑3 beats. | Smooth transition of audio sources. |
| 7 | **Activate** the Delay (pad) on Deck B once the crossfader hits center. | Adds a subtle echo to the new track. |
| 8 | **Adjust** the Delay Mix knob (Knob 2) to 20 % as the track builds. | Enhances the vibe without overwhelming. |
| 9 | **Return** the Filter Frequency to neutral (low) on Deck A (now silent). | Prepares Deck A for the next incoming track. |

By the end of the sequence, you have:

- Seamlessly moved the energy from Track 1 to Track 2.  
- Used EQ (via the filter) to avoid low‑frequency muddiness.  
- Added a tasteful delay that accentuates the new track’s groove.  

Practice this loop with different tracks, tempos, and effect combinations. As you become comfortable, experiment with **Hot Cues** for surprise drops or **Loop Rolls** for creative pauses.

---

## 7. Troubleshooting Common Performance‑Mode Issues

| Issue | Likely Cause | Quick Fix |
|-------|--------------|-----------|
| **Audio drops when switching decks** | Crossfader curve set too sharp, or gain levels mismatched. | Switch to **Linear** curve and set both decks’ gain to 0 dB. |
| **Effect sounds muddy** | Mix knob set too high, multiple effects stacked. | Reduce each effect’s Mix to ≤ 25 % and disable unnecessary slots. |
| **Controller knobs don’t respond** | MIDI mapping not saved or controller not recognized. | Re‑open **Preferences → Controller**, click **Rescan**, then re‑map the needed parameters. |
| **Loop doesn’t exit** | Loop Exit button not pressed, or auto‑loop enabled. | Press **Loop Exit** (often a button labeled “Loop”) or turn off **Auto‑Loop** in the top bar. |
| **Latency (delay between controller move and sound)** | Audio buffer size too large. | Go to **Preferences → Audio**, lower the **Buffer Size** (e.g., from 512 samples to 256 samples). |

If problems persist, consult the **Help** menu or the official Pioneer support forums for device‑specific advice.

---

## 8. Tips for a Confident Performance

- **Start Small:** Begin with two tracks and a single effect. Master the timing before adding more layers.  
- **Use Visual Cues:** The waveform’s beat markers (green lines) help you anticipate phrase changes.  
- **Practice the “Two‑Track Rule”:** Keep one deck playing while you prep the next—this prevents dead air.  
- **Record Your Sessions:** Use Rekordbox’s built‑in recording (found in the top‑right) to capture practice mixes. Listening back highlights where EQ or effect usage can improve.  
- **Stay Organized:** Rename your effect presets (e.g., “Soft Reverb”) so you can locate them quickly during a set.  

---

## Key Takeaways

- **Performance mode** organizes two virtual decks, a mixer, and an effect rack into a single, live‑ready screen.  
- **Loading tracks** is as simple as dragging from the library or using right‑click “Load to Deck” commands.  
- **Mixer controls**—gain, three‑band EQ, and filter—let you balance levels and shape frequencies for clean transitions.  
- **Crossfader** blends the decks; choose a curve (linear, sharp, or custom) that matches your mixing style.  
- **Built‑in effects** (delay, reverb, filter, etc.) add creative flair; start with low Mix values and experiment with parameters.  
- **Mapping effects** to controller knobs or pads gives tactile, on‑the‑fly control; save mapping presets for different genres or moods.  
- **A practical workflow**—play, cue, loop, filter, crossfade, and add effects—creates smooth, musical transitions.  

With these tools under your fingers, you’re ready to turn a simple two‑deck setup into a dynamic performance that keeps the dancefloor moving. Happy mixing!

# Chapter 9: Sync, Beat Matching, and Advanced Mixing

## A Real‑World Moment: The First Drop

Imagine you’re on a small club stage. The crowd’s energy is rising, the previous track is winding down, and you’ve got a fresh banger queued on Deck B. The beat of the incoming track is **exactly** one BPM faster than the one that’s still playing. You have only a few seconds to decide: **Do you trust the Sync button, or will you match the beats manually?**  

This split‑second decision is the heart of beat‑matching. Whether you rely on Rekordbox’s automatic synchronization or fine‑tune the tempo yourself, the goal is the same—creating a seamless transition that keeps the dance floor moving. In the sections that follow, we’ll walk through every tool you need to make that decision confidently, from turning Sync on and off to mastering the pitch fader, jog wheel, phrase sync, and the essential mixing techniques that turn a simple cross‑fade into a polished performance.

---

## Enabling and Disabling the Sync Function

### Where the Sync Button Lives

When you’re in **Performance Mode**, each deck’s channel strip contains a **Sync** button (the iconic double‑arrow icon). It sits right next to the **Cue** button and the **Play** button, making it easy to spot during a live set. Clicking it toggles the deck between **Master** (Sync on) and **Slave** (Sync off) mode.

- **Master Deck** – The deck you control the global tempo from. Its BPM becomes the reference for any other decks that have Sync enabled.
- **Slave Deck** – Any deck with Sync turned on will automatically follow the Master’s BPM and beat grid.

### How to Turn Sync On and Off

1. **Select the deck** you want to act as the Master (usually Deck A).  
2. **Press the Sync button** on that deck – it lights up, indicating Sync is active.  
3. **Press the Sync button** on the other deck(s) you want to follow the Master. They will also light up, showing they are in Slave mode.  

To **disable Sync** on a deck, simply press its Sync button again. The light will turn off, and the deck will no longer track the Master’s tempo.

### When to Use Sync

| Situation | Recommended Approach |
|-----------|----------------------|
| **Beginner practice** – You’re still learning to listen for beat differences. | **Use Sync** to focus on phrasing and mixing techniques without worrying about tempo. |
| **Live performance with tight transitions** – You need rapid, reliable tempo matching. | **Enable Sync** for the majority of tracks, but be ready to disengage for creative control. |
| **Creative mixing** – You want to stretch or compress a track’s tempo for effect. | **Turn Sync off** and manipulate the pitch fader manually. |

> **Tip:** Even when Sync is on, you can still fine‑tune the tempo with the pitch fader (see the next section). This hybrid approach gives you both the safety net of automatic beat alignment and the expressive freedom of manual control.

---

## Manual Beat‑Matching Fundamentals

### Understanding the Pitch Fader

The **pitch fader** (sometimes called the **tempo fader**) is the horizontal slider that sits beneath the jog wheel on each deck. It adjusts the playback speed of the track in real time, expressed as a percentage (e.g., **+6 %**, **−3 %**, **0 %**). In Rekordbox, the default range is **±6 %**, but you can expand it to **±12 %** in the Preferences if you need a wider adjustment range.

- **Positive values** speed the track up (higher BPM).  
- **Negative values** slow the track down (lower BPM).  

When you move the pitch fader, Rekordbox automatically updates the track’s BPM display, but the **beatgrid** (the visual grid of beats you saw in Chapter 6) remains anchored to the original analysis. This means you can see exactly how many **cents** (hundredths of a beat) you are shifting the track.

### Using the Jog Wheel for Fine Adjustments

The **jog wheel** is the circular, tactile controller located above the pitch fader. It serves two primary purposes:

1. **Scratching** – Rotating the wheel while the track is playing creates a classic DJ scratch effect.  
2. **Nudging** – Small, quick turns while the track is in **play mode** make micro‑adjustments to keep the beats locked.

When you’re beat‑matching manually, you’ll use the jog wheel to **nudge** the deck that is slightly ahead or behind. Think of it as a “tiny steering wheel” for the tempo: a light clockwise nudge speeds the track up a fraction of a beat; a counter‑clockwise nudge slows it down.

> **Pro tip:** Keep the jog wheel relaxed. A tight grip can cause over‑correction, making the beats jump out of sync.

### Step‑by‑Step Manual Beat‑Matching Exercise

1. **Load two tracks** – Deck A (playing) and Deck B (cueed).  
2. **Disable Sync** on both decks.  
3. **Set a cue point** on Deck B at the first downbeat (you already know how to set cue points from Chapter 6).  
4. **Start Deck A** and let it run for a few bars.  
5. **Press Play on Deck B** at the exact moment the downbeat of Deck A occurs.  
6. **Listen**: Are the beats aligned? If Deck B is slightly ahead, turn the pitch fader **down** (negative). If it’s behind, turn it **up** (positive).  
7. **Nudge** with the jog wheel to correct any remaining drift.  
8. **Repeat** the process until you can consistently line up the beats within a single bar without looking at the BPM numbers—rely on your ears.

Practice this routine with tracks of varying BPM differences (e.g., 120 → 124 BPM, 128 → 132 BPM). Over time, you’ll develop an instinct for how far to move the pitch fader based on the audible tempo gap.

---

## Phrase Sync and Beat Sync

### Beat Sync vs. Phrase Sync: What’s the Difference?

- **Beat Sync** aligns the **individual beats** of two tracks. It ensures that the kick drums hit at the same moment, but it doesn’t consider larger musical sections.
- **Phrase Sync** goes a step further: it aligns the **musical phrases** (typically 4, 8, 16, or 32‑beat sections) so that melodic elements, vocal hooks, and energy builds line up.

In Rekordbox, the **Phrase** indicator appears as a small **“P”** icon on the waveform display. When Phrase Sync is active, the software automatically shifts Deck B so that its phrase start matches Deck A’s current phrase position.

### Activating Phrase Sync in Rekordbox

1. **Enable Sync** on both decks (as described earlier).  
2. In the **Deck view**, locate the **Phrase Sync** button – it looks like two interlocking circles with a “P” inside.  
3. **Press the button** on the deck you want to act as the Slave. The button will illuminate, indicating that Phrase Sync is engaged.  

When you trigger **Play** on the Slave deck, Rekordbox will automatically **nudge** the track forward or backward to the nearest phrase boundary, ensuring the musical sections line up perfectly.

### Practical Workflow for Phrase‑Aligned Mixing

1. **Identify phrase lengths** – Most EDM, house, and pop tracks use 16‑beat phrases. You can see the phrase markers in the waveform (the vertical lines that appear every 4 or 8 beats).  
2. **Cue at the start of a phrase** – Use a cue point placed at the beginning of a phrase (you may have set these during track preparation).  
3. **Enable Phrase Sync** on the upcoming track (Deck B).  
4. **Launch Deck B** – Rekordbox will automatically jump to the nearest phrase start, aligning it with Deck A’s current phrase.  
5. **Cross‑fade** using the techniques in the next section.

By combining **Beat Sync** for tight rhythmic alignment and **Phrase Sync** for musical coherence, you’ll produce transitions that feel both technically perfect and musically satisfying.

---

## Basic Mixing Transitions

Once the beats and phrases are aligned, the art of mixing comes down to **how** you blend the two audio streams. The three core tools are the **Crossfader**, **EQ**, and **Filter**. Below we break down each technique and show how to apply them in a beginner‑friendly way.

### 1. Fade with the Crossfader

The **crossfader** sits horizontally on the mixer (or the virtual mixer in Rekordbox) and lets you move audio from Deck A to Deck B smoothly.

- **Full left** – Only Deck A is heard.  
- **Full right** – Only Deck B is heard.  
- **Center** – Both decks are heard equally.

**Basic fade‑in/out routine**

1. **Start Deck B** on a beat that matches Deck A (using Sync or manual beat‑matching).  
2. **Gradually slide** the crossfader from Deck A toward Deck B over 4–8 bars.  
3. **Listen** for any clashing frequencies (e.g., both kick drums hitting together). If you hear a clash, use EQ to carve out space (see next section).  

### 2. EQ Blending

Each deck’s channel strip includes a three‑band **EQ**: **Low (Bass)**, **Mid**, and **High (Treble)**. Adjusting these helps you avoid frequency conflicts and shape the tonal balance of the mix.

**Common EQ strategies**

| Situation | EQ Action |
|-----------|-----------|
| **Kick drum clash** (both tracks have strong low‑end) | **Cut the Low** on the incoming deck (Deck B) while the outgoing deck (Deck A) is still playing. |
| **Vocal overlap** (both tracks have prominent mids) | **Reduce the Mid** on one deck to let the vocal shine. |
| **Bright energy boost** (you want a sparkling finish) | **Raise the High** on the incoming deck as it comes in. |

**Step‑by‑step EQ transition**

1. **Before the cross‑fade**, lower the **Low** knob on Deck B to 0 dB (or slightly negative).  
2. **During the cross‑fade**, as Deck B becomes dominant, **raise** its Low knob back to the original level while simultaneously **lowering** Deck A’s Low knob.  
3. **Repeat** the same pattern for Mid and High bands if needed.

### 3. Filter Sweeps

A **filter** is an effect that attenuates (cuts) a range of frequencies, creating a sweeping sound that can be used for dramatic transitions. In Rekordbox, the **Filter** knob is located on each deck’s channel strip (usually labeled “F”).

- **Low‑pass filter** – Allows low frequencies to pass, cutting high frequencies.  
- **High‑pass filter** – Allows high frequencies to pass, cutting low frequencies.

**Simple filter transition**

1. **Engage the filter** on Deck A and turn it **down** (low‑pass) as Deck B starts. This creates a “fade‑out” of the high frequencies.  
2. **Simultaneously**, bring Deck B’s **filter up** (high‑pass) so the incoming track’s highs emerge first.  
3. **Cross‑fade** the decks while the filters are moving in opposite directions for a smooth, evolving texture.

### Combining Techniques

A polished transition often layers these tools:

- **Start with a beat‑matched cue** (Sync or manual).  
- **Apply a low‑pass filter** on the outgoing track to remove its highs.  
- **Begin the cross‑fader** movement while **cutting the low** on the incoming track.  
- **Adjust EQ** mid‑mix to balance bass and mids.  
- **Release the filter** on the incoming track as it reaches full volume.

Experiment with each element individually first, then gradually combine them as you become comfortable.

---

## Timed Two‑Deck Mixing Exercise

### Goal

Develop the ability to **match tempo, align phrases, and execute a clean transition** within a limited time frame—mirroring the pressure of a live set.

### Setup

1. **Select two tracks** of similar genre but different BPM (e.g., 124 BPM and 128 BPM).  
2. **Create cue points** at the start of a phrase for each track (you likely already did this in Chapter 7).  
3. **Choose a mixing point**—the moment you’ll start the transition (e.g., after 32 bars of Deck A).  

### 5‑Minute Practice Routine

| Minute | Action |
|--------|--------|
| **0:00–0:30** | Load both tracks, enable **Sync**, and verify the BPM display. |
| **0:30–1:30** | **Manual Beat‑Match**: Disable Sync, use the pitch fader and jog wheel to align the beats. |
| **1:30–2:30** | **Phrase Sync**: Re‑enable Sync, activate Phrase Sync on Deck B, and trigger Play at the cue point. |
| **2:30–3:30** | **EQ & Filter Prep**: Lower Deck A’s Low EQ, engage a low‑pass filter on Deck A, and raise Deck B’s High EQ. |
| **3:30–4:30** | **Cross‑fade**: Slide the crossfader from Deck A to Deck B over 4–8 bars while monitoring the filter movement. |
| **4:30–5:00** | **Reflection**: Stop the mix, note any timing or frequency clashes, and repeat the routine, aiming to improve each time. |

### Tips for Staying on Beat and Phrase

- **Watch the waveform**: The vertical beat markers (from Chapter 6) provide visual confirmation of alignment.  
- **Listen for the “kick‑kick”**: A clean, even thump every beat indicates successful beat‑matching.  
- **Count in your head**: Even with Sync on, counting “1‑2‑3‑4” helps you sense phrase boundaries.  
- **Use the jog wheel sparingly**: Small nudges are enough; over‑jogging can throw the track off.

Repeating this exercise daily builds muscle memory for both **automatic** (Sync) and **manual** (pitch fader/jog wheel) beat‑matching, as well as the transition techniques that make a mix sound professional.

---

## Troubleshooting Common Issues

| Issue | Likely Cause | Quick Fix |
|-------|--------------|-----------|
| **Tracks drift apart after a few bars** | Pitch fader not set precisely, or jog wheel over‑corrected. | Re‑check the pitch fader position, use smaller jog wheel nudges, and consider re‑enabling Sync temporarily to lock the tempo. |
| **Clashing kicks despite beat‑match** | Phrase misalignment (beats match but phrases don’t). | Activate **Phrase Sync** or manually cue to the next phrase start. |
| **One deck sounds muffled after a filter sweep** | Filter left in a partially closed position. | Return the filter knob to the neutral (center) position once the transition is complete. |
| **EQ knobs feel “stuck”** | Hardware controller not calibrated. | Go to **Preferences → Controller** in Rekordbox and run the **MIDI/OSC Calibration** routine. |

---

## Key Takeaways

- **Sync** can be toggled on any deck; the Master deck dictates the global BPM while Slaves follow automatically.  
- **Manual beat‑matching** uses the **pitch fader** for coarse tempo changes and the **jog wheel** for fine nudges.  
- **Beat Sync** aligns individual beats; **Phrase Sync** aligns musical sections, creating more musical transitions.  
- Core mixing tools—**Crossfader**, **EQ**, and **Filter**—work together to blend tracks smoothly and avoid frequency clashes.  
- A focused **timed exercise** (5‑minute two‑deck routine) builds the reflexes needed for live performance.  
- Regularly monitor both **visual cues** (waveforms, beat markers) and **auditory cues** (kick consistency, phrase feel) to ensure a tight, professional mix.  

Armed with these techniques, you can move confidently between relying on Rekordbox’s powerful automation and taking full manual control, delivering polished transitions that keep the crowd dancing from the first beat to the last.
